analysis.one_liner: Allows individuals to import up to 90-day supplies of prescription drugs from certified Canadian pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in May 2015 and never received a vote, dying in a subcommittee when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the Department of Health and Human Services to write rules, within 180 days, letting individuals import their own prescription drugs from certified Canadian pharmacies. Purchases would be limited to a 90-day personal supply with a valid U.S. doctor's prescription, and the drugs must be the same active ingredient, dose, and form as FDA-approved versions. Controlled substances, biological products, and several other high-risk drug types would be excluded, and HHS would publish a list of approved pharmacies it certifies after checking their licensing, quality testing, and grievance practices [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay high U.S. prices for prescription drugs, especially people taking long-term medications whose versions sell for less in Canada. The bill would let them buy up to a 90-day supply at a time from Canadian pharmacies certified by the U.S. government [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires HHS to issue regulations within 180 days permitting individuals to safely import prescription drugs bought from approved Canadian pharmacies [S2] [S3].

Each purchase must be for personal use in quantities not exceeding a 90-day supply, filled with a valid prescription from a U.S.-licensed physician, and the drug must match an FDA-approved drug's active ingredient, route of administration, dosage form, and strength [S2] [S3].

The bill excludes controlled substances, biological products, infused and intravenous drugs, refrigerated drugs, and other higher-risk categories, and requires HHS to certify pharmacies that meet licensing, quality-assurance, and grievance standards before publishing an approved list [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name prescription drug manufacturers, whose Canadian prices are typically lower than U.S. prices, would lose sales as patients fill prescriptions through certified Canadian pharmacies instead of U.S. drugstores and mail-order plans.

drawbacks.text: Imported drugs would not pass through the FDA's normal inspection and approval chain; the bill relies on HHS certification of pharmacies and laboratory product testing rather than FDA review of each shipment [S2] [S3].

The bill excludes a long list of drug types — controlled substances, biologicals, infused, intravenous, refrigerated, and biotechnology-manufactured drugs — so many patients, including those on newer biologic therapies, would get no relief [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct: patients could legally buy the same medicines at Canadian prices. The design includes guardrails — pharmacy certification, a 90-day personal-use limit, U.S. prescriptions, matching drug profiles, and exclusions of high-risk drug types — which keeps safety risk modest, though certification of foreign pharmacies is still a lighter check than full FDA control over each product. The bigger limitation is scope: many of the most expensive modern drugs are biologic or refrigerated products that the bill excludes, so only part of the drug-price problem would be addressed.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 1, 2015 by Rep. Chellie Pingree of Maine together with Rep. Dana Rohrabacher of California, and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S3] [S5].
On May 8, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, which was its last action in the Congress [S5].
It gathered 7 cosponsors — 6 Democrats and 1 Republican — but never received a hearing, a subcommittee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept exclusive control of U.S. drug sales, and the House's Energy and Commerce leadership avoided a vote that would have put members on record about drug importation.

for.name: Rep. Chellie Pingree
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited bipartisan support including a Republican co-sponsor

for.name: Rep. Dana Rohrabacher
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup of the bill; referred it to the Health Subcommittee, where it stayed

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat and a Republican and drew cosponsors of both parties, 6 Democrats and 1 Republican, so support was bipartisan though small.

industries.note: The bill would let patients buy the same U.S.-approved medicines at Canadian prices, cutting into drug makers' higher U.S. sales. Its defeat left U.S. prices untouched.

industries.industry: Certified Canadian pharmacies and Canadian dispensing operations
industries.note: The bill would have created an HHS certification program and a published list of approved Canadian pharmacies, making them the legal channel for personal drug importation. Certification requirements — five years in operation, quality testing, grievance processes — would favor established operators.

industries.industry: U.S. pharmacies and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Patients filling 90-day supplies through certified Canadian pharmacies would take prescriptions away from U.S. pharmacies and mail-order plans. The bill's limits (90-day personal supply, no resale) kept the loss from being unlimited.
